criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household potable water customer service standards focusing on supply interruptions and reliability attributes (duration and frequency of outages, notification, and temporary alternative water supply) in Adelaide, Australia.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2: the paper does not empirically examine an enacted legal, administrative, regulatory, or tariff rule governing household water access; regulatory General Service Level Agreements and consumer vs. utility property rights are discussed only as conceptual background motivating a methodological comparison of willingness-to-pay (WTP) and willingness-to-accept-compensation (WTAC) elicitation formats, and the authors explicitly note they did not examine WTP for Guaranteed Service Levels. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, even if the hypothetical customer-service-standard property-rights and bill-rebate vs. rate-increase treatments were viewed as touching on a regulatory or institutional factor (borderline plain=yes/unclear, narrow=no), the full-text decision under the plain wording remains exclude because Criterion 4 is also not satisfied.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical data from a drop-off/pick-up stated-preference discrete choice survey of 669 households in Adelaide, estimated using multinomial probit models.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report an empirical outcome of actual water access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. Reliability (interruption duration and frequency) and bill rebates/increases are exogenously assigned hypothetical choice-card attributes, while the measured outcomes are stated choice shares and derived implicit marginal prices (WTP and WTAC valuation estimates in dollars). Descriptive baseline experience of prior supply interruptions (61%) is reported only as a sample summary statistic with no exposure analysis.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households in Adelaide, N=669 respondents across 1,321 WTAC and 1,111 WTP choice observations), experimental exposure/attributes, stated-preference valuation outcomes, and discrete choice experiment study design are all clearly reported.

evidence_quotes.quote: In this paper, we explore the use of choice modelling for obtaining implicit prices for attributes associated with changes in the reliability of household water services.

In this paper, we use choice modelling to derive estimates of willingness to accept compensation for declines in service level quality as well as estimates of willingness to pay for improvements in service level quality.
While this study has estimated the community’s willingness to accept compensation for declines in service levels, it has not examined the community’s willingness to pay for Guaranteed Service Levels.
A total of 835 randomly drawn households from the sampling frame were contacted to fill out the survey and 669 were completed in total.

One of the purposes of this paper is to estimate willingness to accept compensation and willingness to pay for variations in customer service standards. In this case we are interested in the point estimates or the implicit price for the various attributes of service that enter the multinomial probit models.

raw_response.exposure: Between-subject stated-preference survey framing (willingness to accept compensation via once-off water bill rebates vs. willingness to pay via annual water bill increases) and experimentally varied hypothetical service-interruption attributes (duration, frequency, notification communication, alternative water supply, and rebate/rate-increase amount)
raw_response.outcome: Stated choice probabilities across hypothetical service-standard packages and derived implicit marginal prices (willingness to pay and willingness to accept compensation in dollars) for water supply interruption attributes
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban households in Adelaide, South Australia, sampled from streets with three or more water supply interruptions in a two-year period (835 households contacted; 669 completed surveys: 332 willingness-to-accept compensation surveys and 337 willingness-to-pay surveys)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E04, Wrong outcome; also fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading). This is an environmental/resource economics non-market valuation study using a stated-preference discrete choice experiment in Adelaide, Australia, to compare household willingness to pay (WTP) and willingness to accept compensation (WTAC) for hypothetical changes in urban water supply interruption attributes. Service reliability (outage duration and frequency) and bill rebates/rate increases are exogenously varied hypothetical attributes on survey choice cards rather than observed outcomes or enacted legal/regulatory interventions, and the reported empirical outcomes are stated choices and implicit marginal prices ($ WTP and $ WTAC) rather than actual household water access, connection, reliability, affordability, or exclusion. General Service Level Agreements and property rights serve only as conceptual framing, so the study is excluded under both the narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional stated-preference discrete choice experiment (choice modelling survey analysed with multinomial probit models)
